⚠️ Closed alpha — provisional docs. OpenDefence on Kubernetes (opendefence-platform) is in closed alpha and under rapid, breaking development. This page describes a moving target and will most likely be superseded by the documentation that ships with the first public release — treat everything here as provisional, and do not rely on it for a production deployment.

This page maps the opendefence-system namespace — the heart of the platform, where the rmapi hub, the rmui web UI, Keycloak and OpenLDAP live — and explains how they bootstrap into a working core. It is for platform developers and operators who need to know which resource does what; the HTTP contract the hub exposes is documented separately in Core APIs: the rmapi contract.

The core triangle

Three services form the core: rmapi (the Deploy App hub, port 8000), Keycloak (identity, realm RASENMAEHER) and OpenLDAP (user storage behind Keycloak). rmapi drives Keycloak's admin API over cluster-internal HTTP (RM_KC_URL=http://keycloak), and Keycloak delegates its user database to OpenLDAP through LDAP user federation (ldap://openldap:1389). All the namespace's workloads are Linkerd-injected, so every in-cluster hop is plain HTTP (or LDAP on opaque ports) wrapped in mesh mTLS — see Service mesh (Linkerd).

The manifests live in k8s/opendefence-system/{base,overlays/{local,cloud}} and are applied as the opendefence phase of the deploy — after all infrastructure phases, before the product apps. This diagram shows everything the namespace contains.

rmapi — the hub

rmapi is the single Deployment (plus a Service on port 8000) that everything else orbits: it handles enrollment, mints user certificates, answers callsign-validity queries from the edge, and orchestrates the product integrations. What it exposes is out of scope here — see Core APIs: the rmapi contract. What it is, in Kubernetes terms:

  • Persistent state on **rmapi-data** — a 100Mi PVC mounted at /data/persistent. It holds the JWT signing keypair (JWT_PRIVKEY_PATH=/data/persistent/private/rm_jwtsign.key, public keys under /data/persistent/public), with the key passphrase JWT_PRIVKEY_PASS injected from the rmapi-runtime-secrets ExternalSecret. Lose this PVC and every JWT the deployment has issued becomes unverifiable.
  • Kubernetes-native certificate minting — the rmapi ServiceAccount is bound to a Role granting create/get/list/watch/delete on cert-manager.io certificaterequests (plus read access to ConfigMaps). With RM_CERT_BACKEND=cert_manager and RM_CERT_MANAGER_ISSUER_NAME=intermediate-ca-issuer, rmapi mints per-user client certificates directly through cert-manager instead of running its own CA. The chain behind that issuer is covered in PKI & trust.
  • The revocation backstop — rmapi hosts /api/v1/internal/callsign-validity/check, which the Traefik callsign-validity plugin calls (authenticated by the shared Validity-Secret header from callsign-validity-shared-secret) for mTLS requests at the edge. Details in Edge mTLS & callsign checks.
  • CA-bundle trust bootstrap — the shared kustomize component k8s/_shared/rmapi-container-init mounts a container-init.sh (self-described in-repo as a hack) that runs at container start: it creates the persistent key directories, copies any provided JWT public keys, and installs the trust-manager bundle from /pvarki-ca/opendefence-ca-cert.pem into the OS trust store via update-ca-certificates, so outbound TLS from rmapi trusts the deployment's own CA chain.
  • The product registry at **/pvarki** — the kraftwerk-rasenmaeher-init ConfigMap, described below.

At the edge, rmapi is reachable at https://<domain>/api (no client cert) and https://mtls.<domain>/api (client-cert routes) via Traefik IngressRoutes — see Ingress & network edge.

rmui — the web UI

rmui is a static single-page UI served by an unprivileged nginx (container port 8080, Service port 80). Its IngressRoute owns the root domain: Host(<domain>) routes to rmui:80, while the sibling rmapi IngressRoute carves out PathPrefix(/api) on the same host. A second rmui-mtls IngressRoute serves the mtls.<domain> host behind the mtls-chain middleware, with a small mtls-ca-redirect Middleware bouncing /ca* paths back to the base domain. All application logic lives in rmapi; rmui is presentation only.

Keycloak

Keycloak (ghcr.io/pvarki/keycloak-server, started with start --optimized, strategy Recreate) is deliberately the odd one out at the network edge: it terminates its own TLS on port 9443, published as a **hostPort**, bypassing Traefik entirely. That is what kc.<domain>:9443 points at. The pvarki image bakes in --https-client-auth=request, so Keycloak can ask for client certificates itself; its truststore is the trust-manager ca-bundle ConfigMap mounted at /trust (KC_TRUSTSTORE_PATHS=/trust/ca-cert.pem). Because Keycloak handles this TLS itself, 9443 is declared a Linkerd opaque port. Plain HTTP on 8080 stays available in-cluster — that is what the health probes and rmapi's RM_KC_URL=http://keycloak use.

The server certificate comes from a cert-manager Certificate named keycloak (secret keycloak-tls, dnsNames kc.<domain> and mtls.kc.<domain>): the local overlay issues it from the internal ca-issuer ClusterIssuer, while the cloud overlay switches to letsencrypt-http01-production so browsers trust the host.

State lives in the keycloak-postgres CNPG cluster (single instance, 5Gi); the Deployment consumes the operator-generated keycloak-postgres-app credentials Secret.

Realm bootstrap is fully declarative. The keycloak-init Job runs keycloak-config-cli against https://keycloak:9443 and imports the RASENMAEHER realm from the keycloak-config ConfigMap, generated from two files: 01_base.json (the realm itself — clients, roles, and the LDAP user federation component) and 02_flows.json (customized authentication flows; their internals are out of scope here). IMPORT_VAR_SUBSTITUTION_ENABLED=true lets the JSON pull live values from the Job's environment, e.g. the LDAP admin password from the keycloak-ldap-admin Secret and LDAP_CONNECTION_URL=ldap://openldap:1389. The Job has backoffLimit: 100 — retrying until Keycloak is actually up is its wait loop — and cleans itself up two hours after finishing (ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 7200).

The imported federation makes OpenLDAP the system of record for users: WRITABLE edit mode, binding as cn=admin,dc=example,dc=org, users under ou=users,dc=example,dc=org.

OpenLDAP

openldap (ghcr.io/pvarki/openldap-server, strategy Recreate) serves LDAP on 1389 and LDAPS on 1636, both declared Linkerd opaque ports. The directory root is dc=example,dc=org, anonymous binds are disabled, and TLS uses the openldap-tls Certificate (issued by ca-issuer) with the trust-manager ca-bundle as CA. Data persists on the openldap-data PVC.

Seeding is handled by a postStart lifecycle hook: it polls slapd until it answers, then — only if the base DN does not already exist — runs ldapadd with /ldif/init.ldif from the openldap-ldif ConfigMap, creating the minimal skeleton dc=example,dc=org, ou=users and ou=groups. Actual user entries are written later by Keycloak through the writable federation.

Two consumers depend on this directory:

  • Keycloak — via the LDAP user federation imported by keycloak-init (above).
  • TAK server — TAK authenticates its clients against the same directory. The app-tak namespace obtains the LDAP admin credentials through the cross-namespace secret-sharing pattern: this namespace defines a tak-ldap-secret-reader Role/RoleBinding for a ServiceAccount living in app-tak, and an ExternalSecret over there mirrors keycloak-ldap-admin in. The pattern is detailed in Data & secrets.

How the namespace bootstraps

The opendefence phase is the fifth of six deploy phases — by the time it applies, the infrastructure it depends on (CloudNativePG, External Secrets, cert-manager, trust-manager, Traefik, Linkerd) has already been applied, with explicit rollout gates on the CNPG, cert-manager, External Secrets, trust-manager and Linkerd operators (Traefik is applied in phase 1 but not gated on). The taskfile then applies this namespace and blocks before the apps phase on two rollout gates: deployment/rmapi (180s timeout) and deployment/keycloak (300s). The sequence inside the phase:

blocks.html:
Nothing here is event-driven orchestration — it is ordinary Kubernetes convergence. Pods that reference not-yet-existing Secrets stay pending until ESO and CNPG create them, and keycloak-init brute-forces readiness by retrying. One cross-phase wrinkle worth knowing: callsign-validity-shared-secret is created in this phase, but Traefik (phase 1) already references a mirrored copy in traefik-system whose mirroring machinery ships in phase 2 — the mirror converges within its 20-second refresh interval once this phase lands the source Secret.

The product registry

How does the hub find the spokes? Not through discovery — through a mounted file. The kraftwerk-rasenmaeher-init ConfigMap (generated per overlay from files/kraftwerk-rasenmaeher-init.json) is mounted into rmapi at /pvarki and maps each product to its in-cluster integration API plus the Linkerd identity rmapi should expect on the other end:

Product In-cluster API Expected Linkerd identity (certcn)
tak http://tak-server.app-tak.svc.cluster.local:8003/ tak.app-tak.serviceaccount.identity.linkerd.cluster.local
mtx http://mtx-server-internal.app-mtx.svc.cluster.local:8005/ mtx.app-mtx.serviceaccount.identity.linkerd.cluster.local
matrix http://matrix.app-matrix.svc.cluster.local:8012/ matrix.app-matrix.serviceaccount.identity.linkerd.cluster.local

blocks.html:
The trust is mutual and pinned: rmapi verifies each product's mesh identity against the certcn in this registry (MTLS_TRUST_L5D=true), and each product mounts its own kraftwerk-init.json pointing back at http://rmapi.opendefence-system.svc.cluster.local:8000/ with rmapi's identity pinned in turn. The full spoke-side contract — what a product must mount, expose and verify — is covered in Integration pattern. Note that app-battlelog deploys in the apps phase but is not in this registry; it sits outside the hub-and-spoke wiring (and outside the mesh).

In the cloud overlay the registry file is Zarf-templated (###ZARF_VAR_OPENDEFENCE_HOST###), so the same manifests serve any deployment hostname.

Storage & secrets pointers

Everything stateful or secret in this namespace, and where to read more:

Resource What it holds Notes
rmapi-postgres (CNPG) rmapi's database 1 instance, 5Gi — no HA, no backups configured
keycloak-postgres (CNPG) Keycloak's database 1 instance, 5Gi — same caveats
rmapi-data (PVC, 100Mi) JWT signing keypair irreplaceable per deployment
openldap-data (PVC) the user directory written by Keycloak federation
keycloak-init-user (ExternalSecret) Keycloak admin credentials consumed by Keycloak, the init Job and rmapi (RM_KC_PASSWORD)
keycloak-ldap-admin (ExternalSecret) LDAP admin bind credentials shared to app-tak via tak-ldap-secret-reader
rmapi-runtime-secrets (ExternalSecret) JWT_PRIVKEY_PASS passphrase for the signing key
callsign-validity-shared-secret (ExternalSecret) edge-to-rmapi shared secret mirrored into traefik-system

All of these secrets are generated in-cluster by External Secrets Operator Password generators — there is no external vault. The generator pattern, the CNPG credential convention and the cross-namespace mirroring are all covered in Data & secrets.

One honest structural note: the repo's own agents.md flags k8s/opendefence-system/ as a legacy aggregate and an anti-pattern reference — it bundles several services in one component, unlike the per-service layout the product namespaces follow. Read it to understand the running system, but do not copy its structure for new components.
